newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Northern Irish hoteliers build for a peaceful future.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Northern Irish hoteliers build for a peaceful future.

text.p: IRA bombs wrecked Diljit Rana's Belfast restaurants 25 years ago. But not his business spirit.
When Garvan O'Doherty was barely a teenager, guerrillas placed a suitcase packed with explosives in the chief hotel in Londonderry, Northern Ireland's second city.
Today O'Doherty and Indian expatriate Rana are part of a commercial drive to fill a void left by a sectarian conflict that has shown ominous signs of re-igniting after a priceless respite.
They are building hotels.
Experienced hotelier Rana is one of the British-ruled province's best known business figures. O'Doherty is a leader of the hospitality industry in the north-west of the region.
For a quarter of a century Northern Ireland was ravaged by a war that killed 3,200 and devastated town centres with bombs planted by the Irish Republican Army (IRA) in its war against British rule.
Hotels became car parks. Jobs went up in smoke. Tourists trekked elsewhere. Foreign investors recoiled.
Ceasefires by guerrilla foes in late 1994 changed all that. Visitors flocked to the province in record numbers to look at its ruggedly beautiful scenery.
But February's collapse of the IRA truce and summer sectarian clashes rang alarm bells at home and abroad.
Buoyancy about rocketing visitor figures has been clouded by new security and political uncertainty.
Tourism chiefs predict recent instability could mean 100,000 fewer visitors next year compared to 1995, when 1.5 million people came, about 120,000 of them from the United States.

But the industry refuses to stand still. In separate ventures, Rana and O'Doherty have put their money where their instincts lie. Others are doing the same because the demand for hotel spaces continues to grow, industry officials say.
"I am a builder," said Rana confidently as he prepared for the recent opening of his 114-bedroom Holiday Inn Express. It is his third Belfast hotel.
"We bought the site 10 years ago. At that time I foresaw a need for more hotel bedrooms in the city."
Raba says it is the first newly built major hotel in Belfast centre since 1990 when Rana opened the Plaza, now his Holiday Inn Garden Court.
"It's a business opportunity," said O'Doherty about his Trinity Hotel, a 40-bedroom development that opened in mid-October in the commercial heart of Londonderry.
Hotels have been built on the eastern side of the River Foyle which bisects Londonderry, but the west bank commercial hub has been without one for some 25 years.
O'Doherty had the Trinity in mind before the 1994 truces. "The figures stacked up pre-ceasefire."
Punjab-born Rana said the decade to 1981, when the IRA struck with wave after wave of bomb attacks, was the worst.
"They were very bleak years," he told Reuters. "Many restaurants and 11 hotels closed in Belfast city centre during that time. People don't even remember the names of those hotels. I do."
Analysts say political progress is vital for tourism growth.

"The resolution of the present political instability is fundamental to allow the full economic potential of the tourism sector to benefit the Northern Ireland economy," wrote Colm Deignan, a partner with charteredaccountants Horwath Bastow Charleton of Dublin, in a Bank of Ireland-sponsored survey of the hotel industry on both sides of the Irish border.
Five hotels, including projects for Hilton, Stakis and Irish company Jurys, are under construction in Greater Belfast.
Tourism experts say that, along with the Holiday Inn Express, they will add 600 bedrooms to the city's current stock, a 50 per cent increase.
In early 1994 Northern Ireland's Hastings Hotel Group re-opened the internationally-famous Belfast Europa after spending four million pounds ($6.0 million) on redesign.

Once dubbed "Western Europe's most bombed hotel" after 30 IRA attacks, the 12-storey, 184-bedroom Europa hosted U.S President Bill Clinton and his entourage on a landmark visit in late 1995 and has become symbolic of new tourism confidence.
Rana's Andras House Ltd plans two more Holiday Inn- franchised hotels on the outskirts of Belfast.
O'Doherty, who employs 200 in a network of nine pubs, restaurants and a massive disco, has plans for a second hotel if Trinity occupancy rates meet expectations.
A peaceful climate would be icing on the cake. "It would mean we would get a bigger return on current assets."
But he detects signs of a slow-down across the province's hospitality sector in the wake of the past year's volatility.
"You can see it slipping slightly. It isn't a doomsday but people are starting to get uneasy," he said.
Rana is philosophical. "I have persevered and always hoped that some day common sense will prevail and we will get over these difficulties. I still keep that hope."
